title: Layman Pang
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Layman Pang, a householder who studies with Shitou and Mazu, through a short biography written by a wandering monk named Satya. Pang sinks his possessions in a lake, sells bamboo utensils, and asks each teacher who is not attached to the ten thousand things; Shitou answers by covering his mouth. Nomon lingers over Pang's daughter Lingzhao, who answers a question about the hundred grass tips by repeating her father's own words, and over Yaoshan, who calls dropping one thing and picking up another useful. Lingzhao dies sitting on her meditation bench, and Pang recites a verse before dying. Nomon closes with Pang's lines on past, present, and future, and Yaoshan's reminder that time is still in use.

sentences.text: *Non-surpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagatas.*
Good morning, everybody.
Good to see you.
Almost the end of the year.
Nice to have a good gathering together.

You probably have in your mind that there's a million different dharma things you can do tomorrow night, so I hope you'll be able to make us your first stop, and you can go on to other dharma things till midnight.
And I remember you need to get a few things ready if you come to the New Year's [unclear: "Youth"] Ceremony.
In principle, you need a bell and a little piece of paper and a pen, and then a safe way to burn that little piece of paper, a bowl or something, just a little bit of paper.
And then if you want to, you can have a little snack ready for the end.
We'll hang out a little bit like we usually do, at least in this way of hanging out.
Well, I was thinking about the end of the year, like we all have been.
Especially I was thinking about trying to understand a little more, always, about emptiness and wisdom, and how can we hold it all, or is there anything to hold anyway?
How do we respond, right?
How do we respond to our crazy times, our world, our minds, our joyful, beautiful, messed up world?
I was thinking about how often we reference these great lofty priests and teachers as examples.
So we studied Dogen and Suzuki Roshi and all the teachers who showed up in those koan stories.
And that's wonderful.
These are great sources of inspiration.
Pretty much all men too.
I'm not going to solve that tonight either, apparently.
Then I had the good fortune to talk today with Bob Rose.
Joden Bob Rose will be our shuso starting next week, assuming he shows up and doesn't get out of it, in that wonderful ceremony that we'll do with him next Wednesday.

He has a really nice plan for us to really carefully study and digest Master Shi Do's poem, Song of the Grass Shack, same author as in our chant book, The Merging of Difference and Unity that we studied last year.
And he happened to mention something I'd forgotten, which is that among Master Shi Do's students was the famous layman Pong, who was not a priest or a lofty teacher.
He was a really committed practitioner who lived at home with his family, and all four of them studied the Dharma together.
Somebody, I don't exactly know who or how, wrote down little stories about his adventures going around meeting different teachers, and even about conversations with his family about the Dharma.
There's one book about layman Pong, and there's a not too terribly old translation, so there's a modern translation of it.
I was thinking it would be nice tonight to bring up layman Pong and his family as examples of committed practice at home.
Of course the stories are a little quirky.
It's still Zen, still traditional Zen.
But there's a feeling to them, I think, a kind of groundedness and a playfulness and a humor.
If you've had a chance yet to study Norman Fischer's nice book about the six Paramitas, called The World Could Be Otherwise, he mentions humor.
He mentions humor quite a bit, he mentions imagination a lot, he mentions humor.
And he especially mentions humor in the chapter about wisdom: that seeing things with seriousness and humor together is a wise approach, a good approach.
It's an approach in accordance with how things really are, where we don't get so off track, don't suffer so much.
Layman Pong was also famous for his humor, and a lot of the stories are very quirky and funny.
So I just thought I'd share with you tonight a little summary, a kind of abridgment of his traditional biography, and a few of the famous stories in The Collected Sayings of Layman Pong.

It's not very long, and then we can reflect on how that speaks to us as people living at home trying to be serious about practice, as the year turns, as we enter the possibility of a new year, which is of course also just an idea,
it's kind of empty, but a powerful idea, right?
A powerful idea of not 2020.
Appropriately, this little summary was, no, I didn't put it together.
I have these materials, but I didn't put this summary together.
It was put together by a quirky modern monk, kind of like a Layman Pong character, that some of us met, a guy named Satya.
Satya and his little band, a very small sangha based loosely in Portland, live in a similar way to Layman Pong, so it's really appropriate.
They pretty much gave up on having possessions, they choose not to ever work for money, and they live completely on handouts and donations, and the place they practice is donated.
We met them because they were traveling around on their bicycles, because they don't own any vehicles,
and someone had told them something about, I can't remember exactly, I think somebody was maybe offering to give them some land in Whatcom County, so they rode up here to check it out.
I think it didn't work out, because they were back down there.
Anyway, I don't know if you were around for that.
They stayed in the Dharma Hall a couple nights and shared their practice with us a little bit.
Satya and his friends, there were four or five of them, I think it was pretty much a little sangha, maybe some other supporters in Portland.
Satya is a little bit of a scholar, so this is his very nice summary of Layman Pong's life and sayings.
Nice short summary.
So here's what Satya said.
*Master Pong was born and grew up in Xiangyang City, Hubei, the son of a government official.
When his father was transferred to Xiangyang in Wuhan, the young man joined him, and in this new city he married and had a daughter.
Disillusioned with conventional life early on, Pang resisted the bureaucratic life expected of him and managed to avoid getting a government post.
Instead he devoted himself to spiritual practice, building a hermitage besides his house, so he could focus on meditation.
And as he became more committed to simplicity and had been joined in this practice by his wife,*
*they decided to donate their house and make it into a temple and just move into the little hermitage.*
It's like I was thinking of the house I lived at with Janet.
I made a little hermitage in the back, I should have just moved in there maybe.
*And then they loaded all their valuable possessions onto a raft and floated the raft out to the middle of a nearby lake and sank it.
When asked why he didn't just give his possessions away, Pang said that they'd been a source of anxiety for him and an impediment in the way, so why would he wish that on anyone else?*
Why would you burden them with possessions?
*And after this, the Pang family began living off a meager income they could make by crafting and selling bamboo utensils in the street.
And soon the layman, already in his forties, decided to travel and meet Zen teachers.
And he first set off for the Heng Mountains to the north, where he found his way to the practice place of Master Shitou.
So layman Pang asked Master Shitou, who is the one who is not attached to the ten thousand things?*
*Who is the one who is not attached to the ten thousand things?
And Shitou immediately covered Pang's mouth with his hand.
And Pang had a deep realization.
And so the layman stayed on to practice with Master Shitou, and one day the master asked him, "Since seeing me, what have your daily activities been?"
Pang said, "When you ask about my daily activities, I can't open my mouth."
And Master Shitou said, "Because I know you're like that, I'm asking you."*
*So Pang said, "How wonderful, how miraculous, chopping wood and carrying water."*
That's where that saying came from.
So there's two little koans in this first part.
I'll stop periodically, I think, because it's so much, this kind of material.
First koan is a meeting-the-teacher koan.
Pang asks the teacher, Master Shitou, "Who is the one who is not attached to the ten thousand things?"
Shitou immediately covered Pang's mouth with his hand.
How would that be for you?
We ask this question, people ask this all the time: How can I be less attached?
How can I be free?
And the teacher covers your mouth.
How would you understand that?

And then after practicing with Master Shitou for a while, maybe a couple of years or something, the teacher asked a follow-up question, checking on him: "Since seeing me, what have your daily activities been?"
And Pang's answer: "When you ask about my daily activities, I can't open my mouth."
And Shitou said, approvingly, "Because I know you're like that, that's why I'm asking you."
And Pang said, "How wondrous, how miraculous, chopping wood and carrying water."
Just chopping wood and carrying water, right?
Just living day by day.
*Master Shitou approved of this saying and said, "So, are you going to wear black or white?"
The layman said, "I will do whatever is best."*
So, wearing black or white means, are you going to ordain?
Wearing white is wearing layman's clothing, lay robes, and black are the monk's robes.
And Shitou's answer to this is, "I'll do whatever is best."
And it came to pass that he never shaved his head or joined the Sangha.
*Eventually Master Pang, not Master Pang, layman Pang, sorry, traveled to Zhengzhi to meet Master Ma, so the famous Ma, Ma Su.
And he asked his same old question.
"Who is the one who isn't attached to the 10,000 things?"
And Master Ma said, "When you swallow all the water in the West River in one gulp, then I'll tell you."
During these words, Pang had another liberating awakening, and his doubts were resolved.
He practiced with Ma Su for two years and then continued his travels and encounters with other monks and teachers.*
It was a beautiful thing to just keep practicing with your question.
What is your question?
What question do you bring into 2021?
And to ask that of yourself in practice, and ask that of your teacher and your friends, whatever way makes sense to ask it.
It doesn't always make sense to ask it in words, you know?
So this was Pang's question: "Who is the one who isn't attached to the 10,000 things?"
Master Ma replied, "When you swallow all the water in the West River in one gulp, then I'll tell you."
How would you respond to that?
Like you found it deeply awakening to contemplate that level of commitment.
Swallow all the water in Lake Whatcom, and then I'll talk to you.
And when it says he stayed with Ma Su for two years, the way that's understood is he visited him regularly.
He lived with his family.
He's a lay person.
So he must have done a lot of walking.
I don't know exactly the geography here, but I think there's some long walks involved, like walking for a week.
But he didn't have a job besides selling bamboo utensils on the street when they needed money.
So he had that freedom, right?
He had that flexibility.
So there's something in how we choose how to live.
How much freedom does it give us to practice deeply?
Anyway, the story goes on.

*Later he stayed a while on Medicine Mountain with Master Shitou's disciple, Master Yaoshan, and also became close friends with another of Shitou's disciples, the irreverent and free-spirited adept, Dengxia Tianran.

Between excursions, he returned to his wife and daughter in Heng Yang, and both his wife and daughter had also become deeply devoted to the spiritual practice, and all three were eventually recognized for their clear wisdom.
The layman was particularly close to his precocious daughter, Lingshao, whose sharp wit could often outdo her father.*
So there's a bunch of stories about him and his family, especially his daughter.
So here's a couple of them.

*One day in his hermitage, Layman Peng asked Lingshao, his daughter, "An ancient said, 'The bright clarity of the ancestral teacher's mind is the bright clarity of a hundred grass tips.' How do you understand this?
The bright clarity of the ancestral teacher's mind is the bright clarity of the hundred grass tips.
How do you understand this?"
"Such a venerable elder, and yet you talk like this?" admonished Lingshao.
"Well, what would you say?" said Layman Peng.
"The bright clarity of the ancestral teacher's mind is the bright clarity of the hundred grass tips," replied Lingshao.
The layman laughed.*
Another fabulous [unclear: "centrope"].
She said the same words, apparently.
But are they the same words?
When they're said by another in another moment, with another spirit.
*Another time at the hermitage, someone asked the layman if the practice of the way was difficult or easy.* Maybe they had a visitor.
*Is the practice difficult or easy?
"Difficult, difficult," said the layman.
"Like trying to cover a tree in sesame seeds."
"Easy, easy," said Peng's wife.
"Just like touching your feet to the ground when you get out of bed."
"Not difficult, not easy," said Lingshao.
"On the hundred grass tips, the ancestor's meaning."*
So she's referring back to the other time.
So is your life difficult or easy, right?
That's a really good question, isn't it?
Is your life difficult or easy?
If you say difficult, difficult, as hard as trying to cover a tree in sesame seeds, is that really true?
Is it really that difficult?
If you say easy, easy, as natural as touching your feet to the ground when you get out of bed, is that true?
Is it really that easy?
Is it not difficult and not easy?
And on the hundred grass tips, the ancestor's meaning.
So the Dharma is everywhere, right?
That's what the hundred grass tips is: everywhere, absolutely everywhere.
*One day, the layman, lay practitioner Peng, who had studied with both Master Shitou and Master Ma, came to visit Master Yaoshan.* We've met all these characters already.
*The latter master asked him, "What is your understanding of the one vehicle?"
What is your understanding of the one vehicle?* What is your understanding of practice?
*"Every day I feed myself," said Peng.
"How should I know about the one vehicle?"
Yaoshan replied, "Then I'd say you have never really seen Master Shitou, is that true?"
Peng said, "You just drop one thing and pick up another.
What kind of skill is that?"
Yaoshan said,*
As abbot, I have many affairs to attend to."
Pang got up to leave, and Yaoshan said, "Dropping one thing and picking up another is actually quite useful."
Pang said, "Now I see this question about the one vehicle was skillful after all.
I'm afraid I've blundered and gotten lost."
Yaoshan agreed, and I'm sure they both laughed.
Didn't say that, but I'm sure they did.
It was a little more elaborate dialogue.
So the teacher asked Layman Pang, "What's your understanding of the one vehicle?"
The practice, right?
Capital T, capital P, the one vehicle.
And Pang just replied, "Every day I just feed myself.
I'm just living here.
I'm just living here, brother.
How should I know about that?"
And Yaoshan's reply, "Then I'd say you've never really seen Master Shitou," is saying, "You haven't studied very hard, right?
You haven't really paid attention, I see."
And Pang's answer, I think, really impressed him.
Sounds like a criticism, but I think it's a little deeper.
"You just drop one thing and pick up another.
What kind of skill is that?"
And Yaoshan, the teacher, said, "As abbot, I have many affairs to attend to."
So then Pang does the famous Zen answer: leave.
And Yaoshan said, like calling after him, "Dropping one thing and picking up another is actually quite useful."
So we need to live in the relative world, you crazy itinerant practitioner.
We need to live in this relative world.
We need to pick things up and drop them and so on.
And Pang sees the point.
"Now I get this question about the one vehicle, the deep practice, the absolute.
What's skillful after all?
You're right, you're right, dear teacher.
We need the absolute and the relative.
I got a little lost."
It's very humble, you know.
It's strong, but also humble.
They agreed, and they laughed.
Towards the end of his life, Master Pang traveled north towards his birthplace of Jingyang, with his beloved daughter, Lingzhao.
Lingzhao was himself now an experienced practitioner.
And the two found a cave just south of Deergate Mountain in Zhang province and settled there into retreat for the last years of Master Pang's life, Layman Pang's life.
When the Layman was in his final days, he called Lingzhao to him and said, "As the day turns from morning to night, can it be said when it is reached halfway?
As the day turns from morning to night, can it be said when it's reached halfway?
When is it noon?"
So Lingzhao went back out into the garden and said, "It's midday, yet there is some obscurity."
And when he went outside, the Layman saw Lingzhao sitting in meditation on his meditation bench.
But she had died.
Sat down and died.
The Layman laughed.
The Layman laughed in appreciation.
It's a weird one.
And said, "My girl has fitted the arrowhead to the shaft," celebrating her letting go.
After another week had gone by, the governor came by, Governor Yu, came by to inquire about Layman Pang's illness.
And the Layman recited a verse.
*Our [unclear: "hollow desires compromise our hollow desires comprise"] what is something.
The awareness has no substance.
Comprising what is nothing, a good day in the world is but a side effect.*
So, a form and emptiness poem.
*Our hollow desires create what is something.
And the awareness has no substance.
And shows what is nothing.
A good day in the world is but a side effect.*
After reciting this verse, the Layman laid his head on the governor's lap and passed away.
Later, according to the Layman's wishes, his body was cremated and the ashes were scattered in the river.

I assume his daughter's too. [unclear: "In the end of such a little thing said"], monks and laypeople alike mourned the Layman's passing and he was posthumously given the [unclear: "song and name Wei Ma"].
The Layman's legacy includes over 300 poems that are in circulation in the world.
So here's a few of his verses and then we'll see what you made of all that, or maybe there's some little bit of inspiration in there for us.
Here's some verses from Layman Pang.
*My daily activity is not unusual.
I just remain in spontaneous harmony, not grasping or rejecting, nothing left to assert or oppose.
What use are fancy titles and expensive clothes?
The entire mountain is free of even a speck of dust, supernatural powers, and miraculous activity, fetching water and carrying firewood.*
This is like his most famous verse, I think.
*My daily activity is not unusual.
I just may remain in spontaneous harmony, not grasping or rejecting, nothing left to assert or oppose.
What use are fancy titles and expensive clothes?
The entire mountain is free, free of even a speck of dust, supernatural powers, and miraculous activity, fetching water and carrying firewood.*
Here's another verse.
We'll do a couple of verses.
*When the mind is left as it is, the spirit is naturally medicine.
Without a need for medicine, ills disperse of themselves.
When ills disperse, the jewel in the lotus appears.
Don't worry over affairs.
Don't rush around. [unclear: "The why seeing"] wealth and craving, know them to be empty illusions.
Food and clothes sustain body and life, but only for a while.
I advise you to learn being as is.
When it's time, I move to my hermitage and go.
And there's nothing left behind.*
*When the mind's left as it is, the spirit is naturally empty without a need for medicine.
Ills disperse of themselves.
When ills disperse, the jewel in the lotus appears.
Don't worry over affairs.
Don't rush around. [unclear: "The why seeing"] wealth and craving, know them to be empty illusions.
Food and clothes sustain body and life, but only for a while.
I advise you to learn being as is.
When it's time, I move to my hermitage and go.
There's nothing left behind.
The past is already past.
Don't try to regain it.
The present doesn't stay.
Don't try to grasp it over and over.
The future isn't here yet.
The future isn't here yet.
Don't ponder it beforehand.
When the three times are revealed as non-existent, mind is the same as awakened nature.
To quietly function relying on emptiness, this is manifesting profound action.
Not even the least phenomena really exists.
Whatever comes to the eye, leave it be.
No rules to be kept.
No filth to be cleaned.
With empty mind, truly revealed, all things no longer have birth or death.
When you are like this, the ultimate achievement is finished.
It's fulfilled.*
This is really good advice for us at the turning of the year, right?
We're all trying to predict what's going to happen, you know?
We're all upset about what happened and so on.
*The past is already past.
Don't try to regain it.
The present doesn't stay.
Don't try to grasp it over and over.
The future isn't here yet.
Don't ponder it beforehand.
When the three times are revealed as non-existent, mind is the same as awakened nature.
To quietly function relying on emptiness, this is manifesting profound action.
Not even the least phenomena really exists.
Whatever comes to the eye, leave it be.
No rules to be kept.
No filth to be cleaned.
With empty mind, truly revealed, all things no longer have birth or death.
When you are like this, the ultimate achievement is finished.*
So that's a great meditation on time, right?
Past, future, present.
When the three times are revealed as non-existent, mind is awakened nature.
And yet, as the teacher reminded him, dropping one thing and picking up another is actually quite useful.
So it's not like we're done with time.
